articles.title: How to Protect Your IP in China: Answers to the Questions Foreign Companies Ask Most
articles.content:
A manufacturer paid $90,000 for molds used to make its products in China. Two years later, when it needed those molds back, the factory refused to release them. The company ended up paying $200,000 to recover tooling it had already bought. It had a good argument that the molds belonged to it, but it had never signed a tooling agreement covering ownership, permitted use, or the factory's obligation to return them. That omission gave the factory far more leverage than it should have had. A proper agreement at the start would have cost a small fraction of what the dispute ultimately cost.
We see variations of this story all the time. A foreign company shows its product, brand, or technology to a Chinese company and figures it will deal with protection later. By the time it does, the Chinese company already has what it needs and much of the foreign company's leverage is gone. Protecting intellectual property in China is entirely possible, and most of the important protections are far cheaper to put in place while the relationship is still good.
The best time to protect your IP is before the other side has it. That starts with knowing exactly who you are dealing with and being careful about what you disclose. The contracts need to fit both China and the particular relationship, and rights worth protecting in China generally need to be registered there. This post answers the China IP questions foreign companies ask us most often and links to the posts where we cover each subject in depth. Trademarks get shorter treatment here because our China Trademark Registration: The Complete Guide for Foreign Companies covers registration, ownership, squatters, and enforcement in detail.
Yes. Chinese courts enforce properly drafted contracts against Chinese companies. Chinese trademark, copyright, and patent registrations give you rights that Chinese courts, agencies, e-commerce platforms, and China Customs will act on.
The bigger problem is that foreign companies often rely on protections that do little or nothing for them in China: a U.S. trademark registration, a Western NDA, or years of friendly relations with a factory. You need a trustworthy counterparty, contracts written for China and for the actual relationship, and the appropriate IP registrations. We discuss how these protections work together in The Three Keys to Protecting Your IP in China and Internationally.
Find out exactly who you are dealing with. The English name on a website, Alibaba page, or email signature tells you little about the legal entity behind the business. You want the company's registered Chinese name and Unified Social Credit Code and a clear picture of who owns and controls it. You also want to know whether it actually operates the factory it claims to operate and whether the company taking your money is the company signing your contract.
Foreign buyers regularly think they are contracting with a factory when they are really dealing with a trading company or intermediary with few assets. A strong contract against a company with nothing to lose does little good. Our Overseas Manufacturing Due Diligence: A Guide for Avoiding Costly Mistakes explains what to investigate before you send money or confidential information. For larger or riskier transactions, our China Company Reputational Reports draw on Chinese public records and on records available only to China-licensed lawyers.
Tell it only what it needs to quote your job. A factory needs enough information to decide whether it can make your product and at what price. It does not need your complete technical package before it has signed anything. You can almost always get a meaningful quotation without handing over the drawings, formulas, or other information that would let the factory reproduce the product.
Before you give the factory anything it could use to compete with you, sign a China NNN Agreement. File your principal China trademark before your factory and sourcing agent have spent months using the name. We explain what to protect and when in China NNN Agreements: What They Do, What They Don't, and How to Get Them Right.
For some products, the safest approach is to keep one supplier from having everything it needs to copy the product. You might keep a critical component, formula, or final assembly step out of the primary manufacturer's hands, or have different suppliers make different components so no single factory sees the complete design.
A more complicated supply chain brings costs and risks of its own, so this does not work for every product. But sometimes one component, process, or file is what prevents a factory from reproducing your product on its own. Keeping control of that piece can protect you better than another page of contract language.
No. A Western NDA focuses on disclosure: you share confidential information and the other side agrees not to reveal it. With a Chinese manufacturer, the greater risk is often what the manufacturer itself does with the information. It can use your design to make a competing product, sell overruns elsewhere, or use what it learns about your customers and pricing to go around you.
A China NNN Agreement addresses non-disclosure, non-use, and non-circumvention, and it needs to be drafted for China. It should name the correct Chinese company, be written in Chinese with the Chinese version controlling, and provide remedies the factory will take seriously. For a mainland Chinese manufacturer, that usually means drafting for enforcement in China against the actual Chinese company and its assets.
Timing matters. An agreement signed after the factory already has your drawings and prototypes starts from a much weaker position. Our China NNN Agreements: What They Do, What They Don't, and How to Get Them Right and NDAs Do NOT Work for China but NNN Agreements Do cover these issues in depth.
An NNN Agreement is for the first stage of the relationship. It protects your information and business relationships while you evaluate a potential manufacturer and disclose sensitive information. It does not govern quality standards, mold and tooling ownership, subcontracting, production obligations, or what happens when the relationship ends. Once you move into production, you need a China Manufacturing Agreement that governs the manufacturing relationship itself.
One of the most damaging mistakes we see is a foreign company that starts with an excellent NNN Agreement and later signs a manufacturing agreement containing a standard clause that supersedes all prior agreements. If the manufacturing agreement does not preserve or replace the NNN protections, the company can wipe out the very IP protections it worked so hard to put in place.
If the factory will help design, engineer, or prototype your product, settle ownership before that work begins. Who owns the CAD files, tooling designs, prototypes, improvements, and other development work? Can either side use that work outside the project? Those questions belong in a Product Development Agreement signed before development begins.
The High Cost of China Contract Mistakes shows what can happen when a company relies on an NNN Agreement when it really needs a Product Development Agreement. Do I Need a China NNN Agreement or a China Manufacturing Agreement? Usually Both and China Manufacturing Contracts: When One Agreement Is Not Enough explain how the agreements fit together.
We have drafted thousands of China contracts. Nearly all were in both Chinese and English, and not one made both versions equally controlling. There is no good reason to do that. If the versions differ, the parties can end up fighting over what the contract says before they ever reach the underlying breach. We see provisions giving both languages “equal legal effect” all the time in contracts prepared by Chinese companies, and I do not believe that is an accident.
Just this morning, a client sent me a proposed contract from one of its Chinese manufacturers containing this:
This Contract is made in two copies, one for each party. The Chinese and English versions shall have equal legal effect. In case of any discrepancy between the two versions, the Chinese version shall prevail.
The provision contradicts itself. First it says the Chinese and English versions have equal legal effect. Then it says the Chinese version controls if they differ. “Equal legal effect” accomplishes nothing except to create another issue to argue about.
That matters because the foreign company is usually the one that needs to bring the claim. If the manufacturer breaches, the foreign company has to decide whether the amount at stake justifies the cost of enforcement. Suppose the English version supports the foreign company's position and the Chinese version supports the manufacturer's. The foreign company now gets to spend money on lawyers and translators arguing about whether the versions conflict, what “equal legal effect” means, and which language governs the disputed provision. The manufacturer, meanwhile, already has the money, the molds, the product, or whatever else caused the dispute.
Those costs change the economics of a case. A claim worth pursuing under a clear contract can stop making economic sense once the manufacturer has another threshold issue to fight over. Enough friction causes companies to walk away from claims they otherwise would pursue. That is why I am skeptical when I repeatedly see language like this in manufacturer-drafted contracts. Even if the manufacturer ultimately loses the argument, delay and added enforcement costs still work in its favor.
An internally contradictory language clause should also make you suspicious of the rest of the translation. If the drafters failed to reconcile an obvious provision dealing with which version controls, check carefully for less obvious differences elsewhere.
For a contract you may need to enforce against a Chinese manufacturer in a Chinese court, Chinese should control. The manufacturer can read the controlling text before signing, and the Chinese judge can work from the contract itself rather than from a translation prepared after the dispute began. The English version still matters because the foreign party needs to understand and administer the agreement. The contract should simply say which version controls.
We make the case at greater length in Why Your China Manufacturing Agreements Should Almost ALWAYS Be in Chinese and in the “A Worse than Worthless NNN Agreement” section of The High Cost of China Contract Mistakes.
For most manufacturing contracts with a mainland Chinese company whose assets are in mainland China, we prefer a Chinese court. The right forum depends on where the counterparty and its assets are and what relief you are likely to need. You may need the return of molds, an order stopping infringing production, or preservation of the manufacturer's assets. A Chinese court gives you direct access to those remedies against a Chinese defendant. A U.S. judgment adds another enforcement step and can leave you with a judgment that is difficult or expensive to turn into actual relief.
We think highly of CIETAC, but it costs more than a Chinese court, and a CIETAC tribunal cannot itself freeze assets. A request to freeze a manufacturer's assets in a CIETAC arbitration has to go through a court. CIETAC can make sense when a Chinese state-owned counterparty insists on arbitration or when the manufacturer is in a smaller city where its local court may favor it. Hong Kong arbitration also works well in the right case, in part because parties to qualifying Hong Kong arbitrations can seek certain interim measures from mainland Chinese courts.
What makes no sense is automatically choosing New York, London, Hong Kong, Singapore, or Beijing because somebody uses the same clause in every international contract. Too much depends on the defendant, its assets, the likely dispute, and the remedies you will need. We draft the dispute resolution clause last. On difficult transactions, we sometimes have two to five of our China lawyers work through the forum and enforcement issues together. Our How to Sue a Chinese Company covers these issues in detail.
AI-drafted China contracts have been particularly bad on dispute resolution. In the last few months, at least three unrelated companies sent us AI-drafted contracts with essentially the same provision. Each left governing law, forum, controlling language, and enforcement to be “selected by qualified counsel” later. A contract that leaves those choices for later has no workable dispute resolution clause. We discuss that problem in Your AI-Drafted China Contract Says It Needs a Lawyer. Listen to It..
We put contract damages provisions in most of our China manufacturing agreements because they affect how factories behave. When you seek asset preservation, a well-drafted damages provision can give the court a concrete amount on which to base a freeze of the manufacturer's bank accounts. Chinese manufacturers generally know this.
The amount still has to be defensible. Chinese law allows a court to adjust agreed damages that are materially out of line with the actual loss, so an inflated number can make the provision less useful. The better approach is a credible amount tied to a clearly defined breach.
Paying for molds does not settle who owns them, as the client in our opening example learned. Your contract should say who owns the physical tooling and the designs behind it, where the tooling will be kept, who may use it, and when it must be returned.
Tooling disputes usually arise when the relationship is already deteriorating. You want to move production, and the factory suddenly claims an unpaid engineering fee, asserts ownership of the design, or stops responding. By then the factory holds most of the leverage. That is how our client ended up paying $200,000 to recover tooling it had already bought.
Who Owns Your Molds? How Overseas Factories Hold Tooling Hostage—and How to Stop Them and THE Guide to Molds and Tooling in International Manufacturing walk through the contract terms that prevent this.
Usually, yes. We have seen companies learn this when China Customs detained their goods. Your U.S. or other foreign trademark registration gives you no rights in mainland China, and China generally gives priority to the earlier applicant. A third party that holds the Chinese registration for the brand on your products or packaging can have China Customs detain your goods even when none of them will be sold in China.
If you manufacture in China but do not sell there, your strategy can be narrow and defensive. We explain how in Manufacturing in China but Not Selling There? Your China Trademark Strategy Should Be Defensive, Focused, and Fast. Our China Trademark Registration guide covers filing strategy and enforcement in detail.
If your product's appearance is an important part of its value, a China design patent should be part of the discussion. We handle those filings for our clients. A design patent protects a product's ornamental appearance, including its shape, pattern, or a combination of design features, for 15 years from filing.
Timing is critical because China judges novelty against designs already made public anywhere in the world. A Kickstarter campaign, a trade show, or a listing on your own website can destroy novelty unless a narrow statutory exception applies. China does not have the broad one-year grace period some U.S. companies are accustomed to. If you first filed a design application in another qualifying country, you have six months to file in China and claim that earlier date.
Consider Chinese copyright registration when the value lies in the creative work itself, including artwork, packaging, and software. China protects qualifying foreign works without registration, but a Chinese copyright certificate provides useful evidence of ownership and creation. That can help when you ask a platform to remove a listing, ask China Customs to act, or sue.
We have represented many artists whose works are fabricated in China, and for them copyright ownership and registration can be central to the manufacturing arrangement. If a freelancer created the work, do not assume payment transferred the copyright. Establish the chain of title in writing before you send anything to a factory.
China Copyright Law: It Pays to Register, China Copyright Law: The Basics, and Protecting Your Artwork Internationally: What Artists Need to Do Before the Work Travels cover the details. Our China Trademark Registration guide explains how trademark and copyright protection can work together for a logo.
It can, but you should own the Chinese registration and license the distributor to use the mark for its distribution work. A distributor that owns your Chinese registration gains leverage over whether you can replace it or continue using your own brand in China. That leverage tends to show up when the relationship ends.
Your distribution agreement should prohibit the distributor from filing your marks, their Chinese-language versions, or anything confusingly similar in its own name. It should also address what happens if the distributor has already done so. We discuss the problem in China Trademarks and Your Chinese Distributor.
Usually not. A joint venture may need the right to use your technology, brand, or know-how. It does not need to own them. We generally keep core IP outside the joint venture and license the venture only what it needs for the purposes, territory, and period the business requires.
If engineers inside the joint venture improve your technology, decide in advance who owns those improvements and whether either shareholder can use them outside the venture. Once core IP has been transferred into a joint venture, getting it back after the relationship fails is extremely difficult.
Start with employment contracts that address confidentiality and ownership of employee-created IP. Back those contracts with properly implemented company rules and regulations, which carry real weight under Chinese employment law.
A company claiming trade secret protection also has to show it took reasonable steps to keep the information secret. Limit access to people who need it, control devices and credentials, and have a real exit process when employees leave.
Post-employment non-competes need separate attention. Chinese law limits them to senior management, senior technical personnel, and other employees with confidentiality obligations. The restricted period cannot exceed two years, and the employer must pay compensation during that period. Putting a non-compete in every employment contract can saddle you with compensation obligations for employees who never needed restricting. Our China Employee Non-Compete Agreements: Essential Guidelines and Compensation Requirement and China Employment Law FAQs cover the rules.
Your options depend heavily on what you did before the copying began. A China NNN Agreement or manufacturing agreement puts you in a much stronger position if it names the correct Chinese company, is drafted for enforcement in China, and includes a damages provision. Chinese IP registrations add administrative, Customs, and court remedies. Without those protections, the available claims and remedies are usually narrower and more expensive to pursue.
Do not start with an angry demand letter. Preserve the record first: your agreements, WeChat messages, and anything showing when and how the factory received your information. Then determine exactly whom you would be proceeding against. A factory, its trading company, and its owner are not interchangeable even when the same people run all three. How to Sue a Chinese Company covers evidence, asset freezes, and enforcement in detail.
Start with the Chinese trademark record. Find out exactly what was filed, who filed it, which goods or services it covers, and where the application stands. Before contacting the applicant, preserve the evidence you may need for an opposition, invalidation, or other challenge.
If the application is still in its opposition period, act immediately. The current opposition period is three months. China's revised Trademark Law takes effect on January 1, 2027, and reduces the opposition period to two months for applications governed by the new law.
Our China Trademark Registration: The Complete Guide for Foreign Companies walks through the options, including when a negotiated purchase makes more commercial sense than an opposition, invalidation, or cancellation proceeding. Five Practical Steps Foreign Brands Should Take to Prepare for China's New Trademark Law covers the 2027 changes.
If you are about to work with a Chinese manufacturer, do the important work while it still wants the deal. Find out who the company really is. File the China trademark you do not want somebody else to own. Get the NNN Agreement signed before turning over information the factory can use without you. If the factory is helping develop the product, settle ownership before development starts, and have the manufacturing agreement in place before production.
If production is already underway and some of this never happened, do not assume it is too late. Review the contracts you have, search the Chinese trademark register, and find out who actually controls your molds, drawings, CAD files, formulas, and other technical material. Then fix what you can while the relationship is still functioning. Once the factory wants out, or realizes that you do, nearly everything gets harder and more expensive.

Protecting intellectual property in China is entirely possible, and most of the important protections are far cheaper to put in place while the relationship is still good.

The best time to protect your IP is before the other side has it. That starts with knowing exactly who you are dealing with and being careful about what you disclose. The contracts need to fit both China and the particular relationship, and rights worth protecting in China generally need to be registered there. This post answers the China IP questions foreign companies ask us most often and links to the posts where we cover each subject in depth. Trademarks get shorter treatment here because our China Trademark Registration: The Complete Guide for Foreign Companies covers registration, ownership, squatters, and enforcement in detail.

Before You Share Anything

Is it possible to protect IP in China?

Yes. Chinese courts enforce properly drafted contracts against Chinese companies. Chinese trademark, copyright, and patent registrations give you rights that Chinese courts, agencies, e-commerce platforms, and China Customs will act on.

The bigger problem is that foreign companies often rely on protections that do little or nothing for them in China: a U.S. trademark registration, a Western NDA, or years of friendly relations with a factory. You need a trustworthy counterparty, contracts written for China and for the actual relationship, and the appropriate IP registrations. We discuss how these protections work together in The Three Keys to Protecting Your IP in China and Internationally.

What should I find out before I contact a Chinese manufacturer?

Find out exactly who you are dealing with. The English name on a website, Alibaba page, or email signature tells you little about the legal entity behind the business. You want the company's registered Chinese name and Unified Social Credit Code and a clear picture of who owns and controls it. You also want to know whether it actually operates the factory it claims to operate and whether the company taking your money is the company signing your contract.

Foreign buyers regularly think they are contracting with a factory when they are really dealing with a trading company or intermediary with few assets. A strong contract against a company with nothing to lose does little good. Our Overseas Manufacturing Due Diligence: A Guide for Avoiding Costly Mistakes explains what to investigate before you send money or confidential information. For larger or riskier transactions, our China Company Reputational Reports draw on Chinese public records and on records available only to China-licensed lawyers.

How much should I tell a factory before signing anything?

Tell it only what it needs to quote your job. A factory needs enough information to decide whether it can make your product and at what price. It does not need your complete technical package before it has signed anything. You can almost always get a meaningful quotation without handing over the drawings, formulas, or other information that would let the factory reproduce the product.

Before you give the factory anything it could use to compete with you, sign a China NNN Agreement. File your principal China trademark before your factory and sourcing agent have spent months using the name. We explain what to protect and when in China NNN Agreements: What They Do, What They Don't, and How to Get Them Right.

How can I structure production to protect my product?

For some products, the safest approach is to keep one supplier from having everything it needs to copy the product. You might keep a critical component, formula, or final assembly step out of the primary manufacturer's hands, or have different suppliers make different components so no single factory sees the complete design.

A more complicated supply chain brings costs and risks of its own, so this does not work for every product. But sometimes one component, process, or file is what prevents a factory from reproducing your product on its own. Keeping control of that piece can protect you better than another page of contract language.

Contracts That Work in China

Is an NDA enough to protect my product?

No. A Western NDA focuses on disclosure: you share confidential information and the other side agrees not to reveal it. With a Chinese manufacturer, the greater risk is often what the manufacturer itself does with the information. It can use your design to make a competing product, sell overruns elsewhere, or use what it learns about your customers and pricing to go around you.

A China NNN Agreement addresses non-disclosure, non-use, and non-circumvention, and it needs to be drafted for China. It should name the correct Chinese company, be written in Chinese with the Chinese version controlling, and provide remedies the factory will take seriously. For a mainland Chinese manufacturer, that usually means drafting for enforcement in China against the actual Chinese company and its assets.

Timing matters. An agreement signed after the factory already has your drawings and prototypes starts from a much weaker position. Our China NNN Agreements: What They Do, What They Don't, and How to Get Them Right and NDAs Do NOT Work for China but NNN Agreements Do cover these issues in depth.

When Do I Need More Than an NNN Agreement?

An NNN Agreement is for the first stage of the relationship. It protects your information and business relationships while you evaluate a potential manufacturer and disclose sensitive information. It does not govern quality standards, mold and tooling ownership, subcontracting, production obligations, or what happens when the relationship ends. Once you move into production, you need a China Manufacturing Agreement that governs the manufacturing relationship itself.

One of the most damaging mistakes we see is a foreign company that starts with an excellent NNN Agreement and later signs a manufacturing agreement containing a standard clause that supersedes all prior agreements. If the manufacturing agreement does not preserve or replace the NNN protections, the company can wipe out the very IP protections it worked so hard to put in place.

If the factory will help design, engineer, or prototype your product, settle ownership before that work begins. Who owns the CAD files, tooling designs, prototypes, improvements, and other development work? Can either side use that work outside the project? Those questions belong in a Product Development Agreement signed before development begins.

The High Cost of China Contract Mistakes shows what can happen when a company relies on an NNN Agreement when it really needs a Product Development Agreement. Do I Need a China NNN Agreement or a China Manufacturing Agreement? Usually Both and China Manufacturing Contracts: When One Agreement Is Not Enough explain how the agreements fit together.

Should my China contract be in English or Chinese?

Use Both Languages, and Make One Control

We have drafted thousands of China contracts. Nearly all were in both Chinese and English, and not one made both versions equally controlling. There is no good reason to do that. If the versions differ, the parties can end up fighting over what the contract says before they ever reach the underlying breach. We see provisions giving both languages “equal legal effect” all the time in contracts prepared by Chinese companies, and I do not believe that is an accident.

Just this morning, a client sent me a proposed contract from one of its Chinese manufacturers containing this:

This Contract is made in two copies, one for each party. The Chinese and English versions shall have equal legal effect. In case of any discrepancy between the two versions, the Chinese version shall prevail.

The provision contradicts itself. First it says the Chinese and English versions have equal legal effect. Then it says the Chinese version controls if they differ. “Equal legal effect” accomplishes nothing except to create another issue to argue about.

That matters because the foreign company is usually the one that needs to bring the claim. If the manufacturer breaches, the foreign company has to decide whether the amount at stake justifies the cost of enforcement. Suppose the English version supports the foreign company's position and the Chinese version supports the manufacturer's. The foreign company now gets to spend money on lawyers and translators arguing about whether the versions conflict, what “equal legal effect” means, and which language governs the disputed provision. The manufacturer, meanwhile, already has the money, the molds, the product, or whatever else caused the dispute.

Those costs change the economics of a case. A claim worth pursuing under a clear contract can stop making economic sense once the manufacturer has another threshold issue to fight over. Enough friction causes companies to walk away from claims they otherwise would pursue. That is why I am skeptical when I repeatedly see language like this in manufacturer-drafted contracts. Even if the manufacturer ultimately loses the argument, delay and added enforcement costs still work in its favor.

An internally contradictory language clause should also make you suspicious of the rest of the translation. If the drafters failed to reconcile an obvious provision dealing with which version controls, check carefully for less obvious differences elsewhere.

For a contract you may need to enforce against a Chinese manufacturer in a Chinese court, Chinese should control. The manufacturer can read the controlling text before signing, and the Chinese judge can work from the contract itself rather than from a translation prepared after the dispute began. The English version still matters because the foreign party needs to understand and administer the agreement. The contract should simply say which version controls.

We make the case at greater length in Why Your China Manufacturing Agreements Should Almost ALWAYS Be in Chinese and in the “A Worse than Worthless NNN Agreement” section of The High Cost of China Contract Mistakes.

Where should disputes with a Chinese manufacturer be resolved?

For most manufacturing contracts with a mainland Chinese company whose assets are in mainland China, we prefer a Chinese court. The right forum depends on where the counterparty and its assets are and what relief you are likely to need. You may need the return of molds, an order stopping infringing production, or preservation of the manufacturer's assets. A Chinese court gives you direct access to those remedies against a Chinese defendant. A U.S. judgment adds another enforcement step and can leave you with a judgment that is difficult or expensive to turn into actual relief.

We think highly of CIETAC, but it costs more than a Chinese court, and a CIETAC tribunal cannot itself freeze assets. A request to freeze a manufacturer's assets in a CIETAC arbitration has to go through a court. CIETAC can make sense when a Chinese state-owned counterparty insists on arbitration or when the manufacturer is in a smaller city where its local court may favor it. Hong Kong arbitration also works well in the right case, in part because parties to qualifying Hong Kong arbitrations can seek certain interim measures from mainland Chinese courts.

What makes no sense is automatically choosing New York, London, Hong Kong, Singapore, or Beijing because somebody uses the same clause in every international contract. Too much depends on the defendant, its assets, the likely dispute, and the remedies you will need. We draft the dispute resolution clause last. On difficult transactions, we sometimes have two to five of our China lawyers work through the forum and enforcement issues together. Our How to Sue a Chinese Company covers these issues in detail.

AI-drafted China contracts have been particularly bad on dispute resolution. In the last few months, at least three unrelated companies sent us AI-drafted contracts with essentially the same provision. Each left governing law, forum, controlling language, and enforcement to be “selected by qualified counsel” later. A contract that leaves those choices for later has no workable dispute resolution clause. We discuss that problem in Your AI-Drafted China Contract Says It Needs a Lawyer. Listen to It..

Do contract damages provisions make a difference?

We put contract damages provisions in most of our China manufacturing agreements because they affect how factories behave. When you seek asset preservation, a well-drafted damages provision can give the court a concrete amount on which to base a freeze of the manufacturer's bank accounts. Chinese manufacturers generally know this.

The amount still has to be defensible. Chinese law allows a court to adjust agreed damages that are materially out of line with the actual loss, so an inflated number can make the provision less useful. The better approach is a credible amount tied to a clearly defined breach.

Who owns the molds?

Paying for molds does not settle who owns them, as the client in our opening example learned. Your contract should say who owns the physical tooling and the designs behind it, where the tooling will be kept, who may use it, and when it must be returned.

Tooling disputes usually arise when the relationship is already deteriorating. You want to move production, and the factory suddenly claims an unpaid engineering fee, asserts ownership of the design, or stops responding. By then the factory holds most of the leverage. That is how our client ended up paying $200,000 to recover tooling it had already bought.

Who Owns Your Molds? How Overseas Factories Hold Tooling Hostage—and How to Stop Them and THE Guide to Molds and Tooling in International Manufacturing walk through the contract terms that prevent this.

Registering Your Rights in China

Do I need a China trademark if I only manufacture there?

Usually, yes. We have seen companies learn this when China Customs detained their goods. Your U.S. or other foreign trademark registration gives you no rights in mainland China, and China generally gives priority to the earlier applicant. A third party that holds the Chinese registration for the brand on your products or packaging can have China Customs detain your goods even when none of them will be sold in China.

If you manufacture in China but do not sell there, your strategy can be narrow and defensive. We explain how in Manufacturing in China but Not Selling There? Your China Trademark Strategy Should Be Defensive, Focused, and Fast. Our China Trademark Registration guide covers filing strategy and enforcement in detail.

Should I file a China design patent?

If your product's appearance is an important part of its value, a China design patent should be part of the discussion. We handle those filings for our clients. A design patent protects a product's ornamental appearance, including its shape, pattern, or a combination of design features, for 15 years from filing.

Timing is critical because China judges novelty against designs already made public anywhere in the world. A Kickstarter campaign, a trade show, or a listing on your own website can destroy novelty unless a narrow statutory exception applies. China does not have the broad one-year grace period some U.S. companies are accustomed to. If you first filed a design application in another qualifying country, you have six months to file in China and claim that earlier date.

Should I register copyrights in China?

Consider Chinese copyright registration when the value lies in the creative work itself, including artwork, packaging, and software. China protects qualifying foreign works without registration, but a Chinese copyright certificate provides useful evidence of ownership and creation. That can help when you ask a platform to remove a listing, ask China Customs to act, or sue.

We have represented many artists whose works are fabricated in China, and for them copyright ownership and registration can be central to the manufacturing arrangement. If a freelancer created the work, do not assume payment transferred the copyright. Establish the chain of title in writing before you send anything to a factory.

China Copyright Law: It Pays to Register, China Copyright Law: The Basics, and Protecting Your Artwork Internationally: What Artists Need to Do Before the Work Travels cover the details. Our China Trademark Registration guide explains how trademark and copyright protection can work together for a logo.

Partners, Distributors, and Employees

Can my Chinese distributor register my trademark for me?

It can, but you should own the Chinese registration and license the distributor to use the mark for its distribution work. A distributor that owns your Chinese registration gains leverage over whether you can replace it or continue using your own brand in China. That leverage tends to show up when the relationship ends.

Your distribution agreement should prohibit the distributor from filing your marks, their Chinese-language versions, or anything confusingly similar in its own name. It should also address what happens if the distributor has already done so. We discuss the problem in China Trademarks and Your Chinese Distributor.

Do I have to give my IP to a Chinese joint venture?

Usually not. A joint venture may need the right to use your technology, brand, or know-how. It does not need to own them. We generally keep core IP outside the joint venture and license the venture only what it needs for the purposes, territory, and period the business requires.

If engineers inside the joint venture improve your technology, decide in advance who owns those improvements and whether either shareholder can use them outside the venture. Once core IP has been transferred into a joint venture, getting it back after the relationship fails is extremely difficult.

How do I protect trade secrets with employees in China?

Start with employment contracts that address confidentiality and ownership of employee-created IP. Back those contracts with properly implemented company rules and regulations, which carry real weight under Chinese employment law.

A company claiming trade secret protection also has to show it took reasonable steps to keep the information secret. Limit access to people who need it, control devices and credentials, and have a real exit process when employees leave.

Post-employment non-competes need separate attention. Chinese law limits them to senior management, senior technical personnel, and other employees with confidentiality obligations. The restricted period cannot exceed two years, and the employer must pay compensation during that period. Putting a non-compete in every employment contract can saddle you with compensation obligations for employees who never needed restricting. Our China Employee Non-Compete Agreements: Essential Guidelines and Compensation Requirement and China Employment Law FAQs cover the rules.

When Something Has Already Gone Wrong

My Chinese factory is copying my product. What can I do?

Your options depend heavily on what you did before the copying began. A China NNN Agreement or manufacturing agreement puts you in a much stronger position if it names the correct Chinese company, is drafted for enforcement in China, and includes a damages provision. Chinese IP registrations add administrative, Customs, and court remedies. Without those protections, the available claims and remedies are usually narrower and more expensive to pursue.

Do not start with an angry demand letter. Preserve the record first: your agreements, WeChat messages, and anything showing when and how the factory received your information. Then determine exactly whom you would be proceeding against. A factory, its trading company, and its owner are not interchangeable even when the same people run all three. How to Sue a Chinese Company covers evidence, asset freezes, and enforcement in detail.

Someone registered my brand in China first. Now what?

Start with the Chinese trademark record. Find out exactly what was filed, who filed it, which goods or services it covers, and where the application stands. Before contacting the applicant, preserve the evidence you may need for an opposition, invalidation, or other challenge.

If the application is still in its opposition period, act immediately. The current opposition period is three months. China's revised Trademark Law takes effect on January 1, 2027, and reduces the opposition period to two months for applications governed by the new law.

Our China Trademark Registration: The Complete Guide for Foreign Companies walks through the options, including when a negotiated purchase makes more commercial sense than an opposition, invalidation, or cancellation proceeding. Five Practical Steps Foreign Brands Should Take to Prepare for China's New Trademark Law covers the 2027 changes.

Where to Start

If you are about to work with a Chinese manufacturer, do the important work while it still wants the deal. Find out who the company really is. File the China trademark you do not want somebody else to own. Get the NNN Agreement signed before turning over information the factory can use without you. If the factory is helping develop the product, settle ownership before development starts, and have the manufacturing agreement in place before production.

If production is already underway and some of this never happened, do not assume it is too late. Review the contracts you have, search the Chinese trademark register, and find out who actually controls your molds, drawings, CAD files, formulas, and other technical material. Then fix what you can while the relationship is still functioning. Once the factory wants out, or realizes that you do, nearly everything gets harder and more expensive.

The post How to Protect Your IP in China: Answers to the Questions Foreign Companies Ask Most appeared first on Harris Sliwoski LLP.

articles.title: When AI Tells You What Legal Work You Need
articles.content:
A recent article in The Verge described something more businesses are encountering: customers trusting AI over the person standing in front of them. A restaurant customer with a shellfish allergy argues with a server because ChatGPT says a dish should be safe. Sommeliers get asked for wines that do not exist. Park visitors arrive with AI-generated itineraries that make no geographic sense and question the ranger who explains why. At my law firm, we see our own version of this all the time.
I want people to use AI before they call a lawyer. I use it too, and it is useful for learning terminology, spotting issues, and figuring out what to ask. A business owner who spends an hour learning about China trademarks, manufacturing agreements, NNN agreements, patents, or due diligence before speaking with a lawyer will usually have a better conversation.
The problem begins when research hardens into a conclusion. Increasingly, prospective clients do not come to us saying, “Here is what we are doing in China. How should we protect ourselves?” They come saying, “We need twelve contracts,” or “We need ten China trademarks,” or “We need a trademark, a copyright, and a patent.” Many of our China manufacturing inquiries are shorter still: “I need an NNN Agreement. Fast.” Before we quote or take on any of that work, we want to know why the client thinks it needs it.
None of this started with AI. In the early years of our China practice, U.S. companies sometimes came to us after falling out with their Chinese lawyers. One exchange from those years has stayed with me. A U.S. company wanted to pursue a particular strategy in China because Nike was doing something similar, and it told its Chinese lawyer exactly that. Its Chinese lawyer followed the client’s instructions. About a year later, the strategy had become a disaster, and the company went back to its lawyer to complain. Her response was essentially, “I knew this would be a disaster.” The company asked the obvious question: “Then why did we do it?” Her answer: “Because you told me that you wanted to.” I could tell you at least ten variations on this same theme. Back then, many of the Chinese lawyers we encountered did exactly what their clients told them to do. We used to say they saw themselves more as scriveners than as lawyers.
If a client tells me Nike is doing something and therefore it wants to do the same thing, I want to know why Nike is doing it, whether the client’s circumstances bear any resemblance to Nike’s, and, most importantly, exactly what it is the client is trying to accomplish. Because nine times out of ten, it is what the client is trying to accomplish that tells us as lawyers what we should do. The same applies when someone tells us it needs twelve contracts, ten trademarks, or a patent. Before filling the list, a lawyer should decide whether it makes sense in the first place.
AI has made this far more common because it can turn a premise into a polished legal plan in seconds. Hallucinations get the headlines, but the trickier cases are the ones where nearly everything in the plan is true. NNN Agreements are useful, tooling provisions matter, and Product Development Agreements solve problems NNN Agreements do not. But a plan built entirely from true statements can still be wrong for the company asking.
I recently received a thirteen-page document explaining how a startup wanted to structure itself. The plan supposedly came straight from Apple’s playbook, but it was clear to me that it came from AI’s version of Apple’s playbook. We do not do complex tax structuring, and I am not qualified to judge the tax merits of the plan. But I read all thirteen pages out of curiosity anyway, and two practical problems were immediately obvious. The structure would likely cost millions of dollars to set up and millions more to maintain, and this was for a startup that had yet to earn a dollar. I call this the tail wagging the dog. I wrote back and, only half joking, suggested they hire the firm that designed Apple’s structure. At least those lawyers would not have to charge them to reinvent it.
Apple, Nike, and other multinationals have enormous revenues, worldwide operations, in-house lawyers, tax departments, compliance teams, and business problems that bear little resemblance to those of a startup. A structure that saves a Fortune 100 company hundreds of millions of dollars can be ruinously expensive for a business still trying to make its first sale. AI can tell a startup what Apple does without ever asking whether Apple’s reasons have anything to do with that startup’s business.
Another recent inquiry came from a small company that wanted to protect its IP and buy products from China. After consulting AI, it had concluded that it needed twelve different contracts before it could safely proceed, and it wanted us to prepare all twelve. I wrote back explaining that in nearly 25 years of China manufacturing work, I could recall only two clients for whom we had prepared as many as four of the agreements on its list, and both were Fortune 100 companies. Some transactions really do require a stack of agreements, but the transaction should drive the documents. Starting with twelve and then hunting for reasons to justify all twelve gets it backward. The company never wrote back.
We receive roughly twenty requests a week for China NNN Agreements (AI often tells companies to come to us for these, so thank you, AI), and many of them arrive with a deadline and no explanation. Before taking the work, we ask what the company is doing and what it is trying to protect. In at least half the situations where someone tells us it needs an NNN Agreement, we conclude that the agreement would have little or no value for what the company is actually doing.
Most of the time, the reason prospective clients give for needing an NNN Agreement is little more than that they want to protect their product. When we ask what about their product merits protection, they often either admit they do not know or say they do not want someone selling their product under their brand name. For most consumer products companies, the greater risk is someone registering their brand as a China trademark, not someone misusing their confidential information. For this reason the better (and less expensive) first step is often a China trademark registration. Oftentimes, especially for a company just starting out, the smartest product protections cost nothing. One example is using an email address that does not reveal the brand name until the China trademark has been filed. Another is not revealing the product’s “secret sauce” until you have reduced the number of potential manufacturers for your product.
Some companies get irritated when we tell them they do not need an NNN Agreement and write back that they will just find someone who will give them one without questioning what they know. They can. What they will not get is anyone asking whether the agreement protects anything, or whether its Chinese version, the one a Chinese court will rely on, says what the English version says.
NNN Agreements can be extremely valuable. A company preparing to disclose sensitive information to prospective Chinese manufacturers often has good reason to use one. But a company buying an off-the-shelf product may have no meaningful confidential information to protect. Another company may already have disclosed everything months earlier. Many companies produce products that can easily be duplicated once they are out in the marketplace, and it is not worth it to them to pay thousands of dollars for protection against just one company. Once a manufacturer has been selected, the relevant protections may belong in a comprehensive manufacturing agreement instead. We could sell more NNN Agreements by taking every inquiry at face value. We would also be selling some people documents they do not need.
Sometimes the contract itself is fine; it just addresses the wrong risk. One company came to us after a product-development relationship with a Chinese manufacturer had gone badly. It had an NNN Agreement and believed its IP was protected. The Chinese company, however, was doing more than receiving confidential information. It was helping develop the product. As the project progressed, the manufacturer began asserting rights in the newly created IP and demanding more money to continue. The NNN Agreement did what it was meant to do, but the company had never put in place a Product Development Agreement addressing ownership of the design work, engineering, CAD files, improvements, and other IP created during the relationship.
By the time the company contacted us, the relationship had deteriorated so badly that our advice was not to buy another contract from us. We told the company to move its development and production elsewhere. It did not like that answer, and I understood why. A new agreement would have been easier to accept, but it would not have fixed what was already broken. Another company came to us after spending three years developing a product with one of China’s largest and best-known manufacturers, which was now claiming that the product belonged entirely to it. We conducted extensive research and told the company that the manufacturer was almost certainly right.
The order of the work matters too. We see companies spend substantial amounts on manufacturing agreements, corporate structures, patent filings, and IP strategies before anyone has done basic due diligence on the company that will receive their money, product designs, molds, or other critical assets. Years ago, we conducted due diligence on a Chinese manufacturer for a company considering buying from it. What we found led us to strongly recommend that our client not proceed. About a week later, an unrelated company contacted us about that same manufacturer. It had wired more than $1 million roughly six months earlier and had received no product.
Another company once called us after spending six months and about $500,000 researching China’s credit-reporting market. It was now ready to enter China as a credit-reporting agency. I got off the phone and said to one of our other China lawyers, “I thought foreign companies couldn’t do credit reporting in China.” He said, “That’s what I thought too.” About fifteen minutes later, we had confirmed it. I called the company back and explained that the business it had spent six months and half a million dollars preparing to launch was not one it could legally operate in China. My explanation was followed by about two minutes of complete silence.
Our due diligence client did not need a better manufacturing agreement. It needed to stay away from that manufacturer. No contract would have made that company reliable. The credit-reporting company did not need a cleverer China market-entry strategy. It needed somebody to ask, six months and $500,000 earlier, whether China would allow it to conduct that business at all.
One of our lawyers once told a client who wanted to invest $2 million in a company supposedly run by a relative of Chairman Mao that the two of them should instead go to Las Vegas and bet the money on red. His chances of getting it back would be considerably better, our lawyer told him, and they would both have a lot more fun. The client hired another law firm and went ahead with the deal anyway. Later, he asked whether we would try to recover his millions on a contingency fee. I remember thinking we would not take that case even on a 300 percent contingency.
Sometimes the most valuable thing a lawyer can say is, “Do not do this deal.” Other times it is, “You cannot do this business here.” Either answer is worth a lot more before you spend the money.
Someone asks AI whether a company selling internationally should protect its brand internationally. AI explains all the perfectly sensible reasons why international trademark protection matters. The company then contacts us and says it wants a “worldwide trademark.” We explain that there is no single trademark registration that gives a company protection everywhere and ask where it actually wants protection. The answer is often “everywhere.” I usually tell them, “Fine. That will cost you around a million dollars.” That very quickly changes the conversation.
I might then ask whether the company is willing to spend $15,000 protecting its brand in Afghanistan. So far, nobody has said yes. At that point I segue into asking where its products are made, where it sells today, where meaningful sales are likely in the near future, and where trademark squatting or counterfeiting presents a real risk. For many smaller companies, we eventually settle on one to three countries. We also manage trademark portfolios for sophisticated companies whose protection covers the European Union plus another ten, twenty, or thirty countries. Those businesses have the international footprint and the revenue to justify that coverage.
We have registered trademarks in some very small countries over the years, but as far as I know we have never filed one in Andorra or San Marino. Trademark protection should track where a company operates, where it is going, what it stands to lose, and what it can sensibly spend. “Protect our brand everywhere” sounds prudent until somebody puts a price on everywhere.
The company that tells us it needs ten China trademarks usually manufactures in China and sells everywhere else. It does need its brand registered in China. But AI often tells it to file a Chinese-character version as well, along with multiple classes and subclasses and defensive filings for confusingly similar variations. All of this might make sense for a company that is selling its product in China, but most of the time a company that will only be manufacturing in China needs only one trademark. It is not that AI got it wrong; it is that the AI user did not know enough to provide AI with the full story.
The same issue comes up when a prospective client tells us it needs a China trademark, a copyright, and a patent. We ask what the copyright will protect, and they do not know. We ask what they intend to patent, and they are not sure. Then they tell us someone on Fiverr will get them all three for about what we charge for one trademark, and they ask why they should not do that. That comparison completely misses what they will actually be paying for with a law firm, which is figuring out what, if anything, should be filed. Trademarks, copyrights, and patents protect different things, and for many companies a good contract matters more than any of them. Some need several forms of protection. Others need none. Most need more than a trademark filed by someone on Fiverr; they need the right trademark for their situation.
One recent Google reviewer contacted us for a second opinion about serving a defendant in China under the Hague Service Convention. She had already hired a service provider but was worried about how long the process was taking. I explained the delay and told her what I thought she should do next, which was to give the existing process more time rather than hire our law firm. She left us a five-star review and specifically mentioned that advice.
Another person contacted me about an estate involving property in the Philippines. I explained her options, gave her the names of some good lawyers I know in the Philippines, and told her that we would be glad to help on an hourly basis but that she would probably be fine finding the right lawyer herself. She found someone without hiring us and later wrote that I had gone out of my way to help even though I knew she would not become my client. A small-business client described our role another way: helping the company figure out “what level of legal service we might need.”
I am proud of those reviews because they describe the kind of lawyer I want to be and the kind of law firm we try to run. We are a business; of course we need paying clients. But if an NNN Agreement will not help someone, we should not sell one. The same goes when a cheaper solution is enough or when the person does not need a lawyer at all.
My reason for this is personal. I have two children, both now adults, and one is a lawyer. Since my oldest was born, I have often asked myself whether I could look my children in the eye and feel good about what I had done. That question applies to practicing law as much as anything else. If I sell someone a legal service I know they do not need simply because they are willing to pay for it, I have taken money I did not earn. To me, that is stealing, plain and simple. I will not charge anyone for a service unless I believe it will provide value.
It also happens to be good business. The firms that keep clients for years are willing to turn down work outside their expertise and tell a client when a case is not worth pursuing. When a cheaper approach will do the job, they say so. Clients remember that. Lawyers have a bad reputation, and some of them earn it. But most lawyers I know want to give useful advice and do right by the people who trust them. The ones who consistently do otherwise develop reputations for it, particularly in specialized practices where lawyers and clients encounter one another again and again.

When AI Tells You What Legal Work You Need

A recent article in The Verge described something more businesses are encountering: customers trusting AI over the person standing in front of them. A restaurant customer with a shellfish allergy argues with a server because ChatGPT says a dish should be safe. Sommeliers get asked for wines that do not exist. Park visitors arrive with AI-generated itineraries that make no geographic sense and question the ranger who explains why. At my law firm, we see our own version of this all the time.

I want people to use AI before they call a lawyer. I use it too, and it is useful for learning terminology, spotting issues, and figuring out what to ask. A business owner who spends an hour learning about China trademarks, manufacturing agreements, NNN agreements, patents, or due diligence before speaking with a lawyer will usually have a better conversation.

The problem begins when research hardens into a conclusion. Increasingly, prospective clients do not come to us saying, “Here is what we are doing in China. How should we protect ourselves?” They come saying, “We need twelve contracts,” or “We need ten China trademarks,” or “We need a trademark, a copyright, and a patent.” Many of our China manufacturing inquiries are shorter still: “I need an NNN Agreement. Fast.” Before we quote or take on any of that work, we want to know why the client thinks it needs it.

A Good Lawyer Asks Why

None of this started with AI. In the early years of our China practice, U.S. companies sometimes came to us after falling out with their Chinese lawyers. One exchange from those years has stayed with me. A U.S. company wanted to pursue a particular strategy in China because Nike was doing something similar, and it told its Chinese lawyer exactly that. Its Chinese lawyer followed the client’s instructions. About a year later, the strategy had become a disaster, and the company went back to its lawyer to complain. Her response was essentially, “I knew this would be a disaster.” The company asked the obvious question: “Then why did we do it?” Her answer: “Because you told me that you wanted to.” I could tell you at least ten variations on this same theme. Back then, many of the Chinese lawyers we encountered did exactly what their clients told them to do. We used to say they saw themselves more as scriveners than as lawyers.

If a client tells me Nike is doing something and therefore it wants to do the same thing, I want to know why Nike is doing it, whether the client’s circumstances bear any resemblance to Nike’s, and, most importantly, exactly what it is the client is trying to accomplish. Because nine times out of ten, it is what the client is trying to accomplish that tells us as lawyers what we should do. The same applies when someone tells us it needs twelve contracts, ten trademarks, or a patent. Before filling the list, a lawyer should decide whether it makes sense in the first place.

AI has made this far more common because it can turn a premise into a polished legal plan in seconds. Hallucinations get the headlines, but the trickier cases are the ones where nearly everything in the plan is true. NNN Agreements are useful, tooling provisions matter, and Product Development Agreements solve problems NNN Agreements do not. But a plan built entirely from true statements can still be wrong for the company asking.

When a Startup Wants Apple’s Playbook

I recently received a thirteen-page document explaining how a startup wanted to structure itself. The plan supposedly came straight from Apple’s playbook, but it was clear to me that it came from AI’s version of Apple’s playbook. We do not do complex tax structuring, and I am not qualified to judge the tax merits of the plan. But I read all thirteen pages out of curiosity anyway, and two practical problems were immediately obvious. The structure would likely cost millions of dollars to set up and millions more to maintain, and this was for a startup that had yet to earn a dollar. I call this the tail wagging the dog. I wrote back and, only half joking, suggested they hire the firm that designed Apple’s structure. At least those lawyers would not have to charge them to reinvent it.

Apple, Nike, and other multinationals have enormous revenues, worldwide operations, in-house lawyers, tax departments, compliance teams, and business problems that bear little resemblance to those of a startup. A structure that saves a Fortune 100 company hundreds of millions of dollars can be ruinously expensive for a business still trying to make its first sale. AI can tell a startup what Apple does without ever asking whether Apple’s reasons have anything to do with that startup’s business.

Another recent inquiry came from a small company that wanted to protect its IP and buy products from China. After consulting AI, it had concluded that it needed twelve different contracts before it could safely proceed, and it wanted us to prepare all twelve. I wrote back explaining that in nearly 25 years of China manufacturing work, I could recall only two clients for whom we had prepared as many as four of the agreements on its list, and both were Fortune 100 companies. Some transactions really do require a stack of agreements, but the transaction should drive the documents. Starting with twelve and then hunting for reasons to justify all twelve gets it backward. The company never wrote back.

“I Need a China NNN Agreement. Fast.”

We receive roughly twenty requests a week for China NNN Agreements (AI often tells companies to come to us for these, so thank you, AI), and many of them arrive with a deadline and no explanation. Before taking the work, we ask what the company is doing and what it is trying to protect. In at least half the situations where someone tells us it needs an NNN Agreement, we conclude that the agreement would have little or no value for what the company is actually doing.

Most of the time, the reason prospective clients give for needing an NNN Agreement is little more than that they want to protect their product. When we ask what about their product merits protection, they often either admit they do not know or say they do not want someone selling their product under their brand name. For most consumer products companies, the greater risk is someone registering their brand as a China trademark, not someone misusing their confidential information. For this reason the better (and less expensive) first step is often a China trademark registration. Oftentimes, especially for a company just starting out, the smartest product protections cost nothing. One example is using an email address that does not reveal the brand name until the China trademark has been filed. Another is not revealing the product’s “secret sauce” until you have reduced the number of potential manufacturers for your product.

Some companies get irritated when we tell them they do not need an NNN Agreement and write back that they will just find someone who will give them one without questioning what they know. They can. What they will not get is anyone asking whether the agreement protects anything, or whether its Chinese version, the one a Chinese court will rely on, says what the English version says.

NNN Agreements can be extremely valuable. A company preparing to disclose sensitive information to prospective Chinese manufacturers often has good reason to use one. But a company buying an off-the-shelf product may have no meaningful confidential information to protect. Another company may already have disclosed everything months earlier. Many companies produce products that can easily be duplicated once they are out in the marketplace, and it is not worth it to them to pay thousands of dollars for protection against just one company. Once a manufacturer has been selected, the relevant protections may belong in a comprehensive manufacturing agreement instead. We could sell more NNN Agreements by taking every inquiry at face value. We would also be selling some people documents they do not need.

Sometimes the contract itself is fine; it just addresses the wrong risk. One company came to us after a product-development relationship with a Chinese manufacturer had gone badly. It had an NNN Agreement and believed its IP was protected. The Chinese company, however, was doing more than receiving confidential information. It was helping develop the product. As the project progressed, the manufacturer began asserting rights in the newly created IP and demanding more money to continue. The NNN Agreement did what it was meant to do, but the company had never put in place a Product Development Agreement addressing ownership of the design work, engineering, CAD files, improvements, and other IP created during the relationship.

By the time the company contacted us, the relationship had deteriorated so badly that our advice was not to buy another contract from us. We told the company to move its development and production elsewhere. It did not like that answer, and I understood why. A new agreement would have been easier to accept, but it would not have fixed what was already broken. Another company came to us after spending three years developing a product with one of China’s largest and best-known manufacturers, which was now claiming that the product belonged entirely to it. We conducted extensive research and told the company that the manufacturer was almost certainly right.

Sometimes the Best Protection Is Not Doing the Deal

The order of the work matters too. We see companies spend substantial amounts on manufacturing agreements, corporate structures, patent filings, and IP strategies before anyone has done basic due diligence on the company that will receive their money, product designs, molds, or other critical assets. Years ago, we conducted due diligence on a Chinese manufacturer for a company considering buying from it. What we found led us to strongly recommend that our client not proceed. About a week later, an unrelated company contacted us about that same manufacturer. It had wired more than $1 million roughly six months earlier and had received no product.

Another company once called us after spending six months and about $500,000 researching China’s credit-reporting market. It was now ready to enter China as a credit-reporting agency. I got off the phone and said to one of our other China lawyers, “I thought foreign companies couldn’t do credit reporting in China.” He said, “That’s what I thought too.” About fifteen minutes later, we had confirmed it. I called the company back and explained that the business it had spent six months and half a million dollars preparing to launch was not one it could legally operate in China. My explanation was followed by about two minutes of complete silence.

Our due diligence client did not need a better manufacturing agreement. It needed to stay away from that manufacturer. No contract would have made that company reliable. The credit-reporting company did not need a cleverer China market-entry strategy. It needed somebody to ask, six months and $500,000 earlier, whether China would allow it to conduct that business at all.

One of our lawyers once told a client who wanted to invest $2 million in a company supposedly run by a relative of Chairman Mao that the two of them should instead go to Las Vegas and bet the money on red. His chances of getting it back would be considerably better, our lawyer told him, and they would both have a lot more fun. The client hired another law firm and went ahead with the deal anyway. Later, he asked whether we would try to recover his millions on a contingency fee. I remember thinking we would not take that case even on a 300 percent contingency.

Sometimes the most valuable thing a lawyer can say is, “Do not do this deal.” Other times it is, “You cannot do this business here.” Either answer is worth a lot more before you spend the money.

The Worldwide Trademark Problem

Someone asks AI whether a company selling internationally should protect its brand internationally. AI explains all the perfectly sensible reasons why international trademark protection matters. The company then contacts us and says it wants a “worldwide trademark.” We explain that there is no single trademark registration that gives a company protection everywhere and ask where it actually wants protection. The answer is often “everywhere.” I usually tell them, “Fine. That will cost you around a million dollars.” That very quickly changes the conversation.

I might then ask whether the company is willing to spend $15,000 protecting its brand in Afghanistan. So far, nobody has said yes. At that point I segue into asking where its products are made, where it sells today, where meaningful sales are likely in the near future, and where trademark squatting or counterfeiting presents a real risk. For many smaller companies, we eventually settle on one to three countries. We also manage trademark portfolios for sophisticated companies whose protection covers the European Union plus another ten, twenty, or thirty countries. Those businesses have the international footprint and the revenue to justify that coverage.

We have registered trademarks in some very small countries over the years, but as far as I know we have never filed one in Andorra or San Marino. Trademark protection should track where a company operates, where it is going, what it stands to lose, and what it can sensibly spend. “Protect our brand everywhere” sounds prudent until somebody puts a price on everywhere.

The company that tells us it needs ten China trademarks usually manufactures in China and sells everywhere else. It does need its brand registered in China. But AI often tells it to file a Chinese-character version as well, along with multiple classes and subclasses and defensive filings for confusingly similar variations. All of this might make sense for a company that is selling its product in China, but most of the time a company that will only be manufacturing in China needs only one trademark. It is not that AI got it wrong; it is that the AI user did not know enough to provide AI with the full story.

The same issue comes up when a prospective client tells us it needs a China trademark, a copyright, and a patent. We ask what the copyright will protect, and they do not know. We ask what they intend to patent, and they are not sure. Then they tell us someone on Fiverr will get them all three for about what we charge for one trademark, and they ask why they should not do that. That comparison completely misses what they will actually be paying for with a law firm, which is figuring out what, if anything, should be filed. Trademarks, copyrights, and patents protect different things, and for many companies a good contract matters more than any of them. Some need several forms of protection. Others need none. Most need more than a trademark filed by someone on Fiverr; they need the right trademark for their situation.

Some of My Favorite Reviews Are From People Who Never Hired Us

One recent Google reviewer contacted us for a second opinion about serving a defendant in China under the Hague Service Convention. She had already hired a service provider but was worried about how long the process was taking. I explained the delay and told her what I thought she should do next, which was to give the existing process more time rather than hire our law firm. She left us a five-star review and specifically mentioned that advice.

Another person contacted me about an estate involving property in the Philippines. I explained her options, gave her the names of some good lawyers I know in the Philippines, and told her that we would be glad to help on an hourly basis but that she would probably be fine finding the right lawyer herself. She found someone without hiring us and later wrote that I had gone out of my way to help even though I knew she would not become my client. A small-business client described our role another way: helping the company figure out “what level of legal service we might need.”

I am proud of those reviews because they describe the kind of lawyer I want to be and the kind of law firm we try to run. We are a business; of course we need paying clients. But if an NNN Agreement will not help someone, we should not sell one. The same goes when a cheaper solution is enough or when the person does not need a lawyer at all.

My reason for this is personal. I have two children, both now adults, and one is a lawyer. Since my oldest was born, I have often asked myself whether I could look my children in the eye and feel good about what I had done. That question applies to practicing law as much as anything else. If I sell someone a legal service I know they do not need simply because they are willing to pay for it, I have taken money I did not earn. To me, that is stealing, plain and simple. I will not charge anyone for a service unless I believe it will provide value.

It also happens to be good business. The firms that keep clients for years are willing to turn down work outside their expertise and tell a client when a case is not worth pursuing. When a cheaper approach will do the job, they say so. Clients remember that. Lawyers have a bad reputation, and some of them earn it. But most lawyers I know want to give useful advice and do right by the people who trust them. The ones who consistently do otherwise develop reputations for it, particularly in specialized practices where lawyers and clients encounter one another again and again.

Use AI Before You Call Your Lawyer

AI often accepts the premise of a question instead of challenging it. Tell it you need twelve contracts and it will help you choose twelve. Ask it to copy Apple’s structure and it starts designing the structure before asking whether a startup should be doing any of that. Ask it to provide you a contract that protects you as much as possible and it will give you a contract that no company anywhere in the world will ever sign.

Then leave room for the answer to change once someone who truly knows this area of law understands the facts. The most useful question you can ask AI is, “What assumptions am I making that might be wrong?” Ask your lawyer the same thing. You are paying a lawyer for judgment, and sometimes the best judgment a lawyer can give you is to do less, not more.
